notes.definition: Fractional distillation separates the hydrocarbons in crude oil into fractions. Each fraction contains molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms and so a similar range of boiling points. The fractions are processed to produce fuels and feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
explanation: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons that are not useful until they are separated. The different hydrocarbons have different boiling points, mainly because they have different numbers of carbon atoms: the bigger the molecule, the higher the boiling point. Fractional distillation uses this difference to separate crude oil into fractions. A fraction is a group of hydrocarbons with similar numbers of carbon atoms, so they boil over a similar temperature range.

First, the crude oil is heated strongly until most of it evaporates and turns into vapour. The vapour is fed into the bottom of a tall fractionating column. The column is hot at the bottom and gets cooler towards the top, so there is a temperature gradient. Any very large hydrocarbons that do not evaporate collect at the bottom as a thick liquid residue.

As the vapours rise up the column, they cool. When a hydrocarbon cools to its boiling point it condenses back into a liquid. Hydrocarbons with large molecules have high boiling points, so they condense low down where it is hot, and are collected near the bottom. Hydrocarbons with smaller molecules have lower boiling points, so they keep rising and condense higher up where it is cooler. The smallest molecules, with boiling points below the temperature at the top, leave the top of the column as gases. Each fraction is piped off at a different height.

Many fractions are used as fuels. These include liquefied petroleum gases (LPG), petrol, kerosene (used as jet fuel), diesel oil and heavy fuel oil (used in ships and power stations). Modern life depends on these fuels for transport, heating and electricity generation. Other fractions, and some of the products from them, are used as feedstock: the raw materials for the petrochemical industry.

The petrochemical industry turns hydrocarbons into many useful materials, including solvents, lubricants, polymers (plastics) and detergents. A vast range of natural and synthetic carbon compounds exists because carbon atoms can form families of similar compounds. Each carbon atom can make four covalent bonds and can bond to other carbon atoms to form chains and rings of different lengths, so there is an enormous number of possible molecules.
keyFacts: Fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions.
A fraction contains hydrocarbons with a similar number of carbon atoms and similar boiling points.
Crude oil is heated until it evaporates, and the vapour enters the bottom of the column.
The column is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top.
Each hydrocarbon condenses when it cools to its boiling point.
Large molecules (high boiling points) are collected near the bottom; small molecules near the top.
Fuels from crude oil include petrol, diesel oil, kerosene, heavy fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gases.
Fractions are also feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
Petrochemicals include solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.
Carbon can form families of similar compounds, so there is a vast array of carbon compounds.

keyTerms.definition: A method that separates a mixture of liquids with different boiling points, using evaporation then condensation in a column with a temperature gradient.
A mixture of hydrocarbons with a similar number of carbon atoms and a similar range of boiling points.
A tall column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top, in which crude oil vapour is separated into fractions.
The change of state from liquid to gas (vapour).
The change of state from gas to liquid, which happens when a vapour cools to its boiling point.
A raw material used to make other products in an industrial process.
A useful substance made from crude oil or natural gas, such as a solvent, lubricant, polymer or detergent.

workedExamples.title: Predicting where a hydrocarbon is collected
workedExamples.question: Hydrocarbon A boils at 125 °C and hydrocarbon B boils at 300 °C. Which one is collected higher up the column? Explain.
steps: The column is cooler towards the top.
A has the lower boiling point, so it stays as a vapour until it reaches a cooler part of the column.
B condenses lower down, where the temperature has fallen to about 300 °C.
workedExamples.answer: Hydrocarbon A is collected higher up the column because it has a lower boiling point.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think each fraction is a single pure compound.
misconceptions.right: In fact each fraction is still a mixture, of hydrocarbons with similar numbers of carbon atoms and similar boiling points.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the column is hottest at the top because hot gases rise.
misconceptions.right: In fact the column is hottest at the bottom, where the hot vapour enters, and cools towards the top.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fractional distillation is a chemical reaction that breaks molecules up.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is a physical process (evaporation and condensation). No bonds within molecules are broken; breaking molecules is cracking.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think large molecules rise to the top because they are 'stronger'.
misconceptions.right: In fact large molecules have high boiling points, so they condense and are collected near the bottom.

realWorld: Oil refineries run fractional distillation continuously, 24 hours a day, producing petrol and diesel for cars and lorries.
Kerosene is used as aviation fuel (jet fuel), and heavy fuel oil powers large ships.
Most plastics, many medicines, detergents and paint solvents start as feedstock from crude oil fractions.
examTips: Use the words evaporate (or vaporise) and condense in the right places: crude oil evaporates in the heater; fractions condense in the column.
Always say the column has a temperature gradient: hot at the bottom, cooler at the top.
Link molecule size to boiling point: larger molecules, higher boiling point, collected lower down.
You only need to name petrol, diesel oil, kerosene, heavy fuel oil and LPG as fuels; for other fractions use the information given in the question.
summary: Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation.
Crude oil is heated and the vapour enters a column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top.
Hydrocarbons condense at the level where the temperature is below their boiling point.
Large molecules are collected at the bottom, small molecules at the top.
Fractions are used as fuels and as feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
Petrochemicals include solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.

questions.question: Which of these is a fuel produced from crude oil?
markScheme: 1 mark: kerosene
questions.explanation: Kerosene is a crude oil fraction used as jet fuel. Ethanol is usually made by fermentation and hydrogen by other methods.

questions.question:
The petrochemical industry uses crude oil fractions as a feedstock.
Which substance is not made by the petrochemical industry from crude oil fractions?
markScheme: 1 mark: iron
questions.explanation: Iron is a metal extracted from its ore. Solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents are all petrochemicals.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a fraction?
options: A mixture of hydrocarbons with similar numbers of carbon atoms
All the hydrocarbons in crude oil that contain double bonds
A compound formed when crude oil reacts with oxygen
markScheme: 1 mark: mixture of hydrocarbons with similar numbers of carbon atoms
questions.explanation: A fraction is still a mixture; its molecules are similar in size so they have similar boiling points.

questions.question: Which description is correct for the hydrocarbons that leave the top of a fractionating column?
options: large molecules and high boiling points
large molecules and low boiling points
small molecules and high boiling points
small molecules and low boiling points
markScheme: 1 mark: small molecules and low boiling points
questions.explanation: Small molecules have low boiling points, so they stay as gases until the cool top of the column.

questions.question: Which two changes of state happen, in order, during the fractional distillation of crude oil?
markScheme: 1 mark: evaporation then condensation
questions.explanation: The crude oil is evaporated in the heater, then each fraction condenses in the column.

questions.question: Why does carbon form such a vast array of natural and synthetic compounds?
options: Carbon atoms form ionic bonds with many metals
Carbon atoms can form families of similar compounds by bonding to other carbon atoms in chains
Carbon is the most common element in the Earth's crust
Carbon atoms can only form single bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon forms families of similar compounds (chains of carbon atoms)
questions.explanation: Carbon forms four covalent bonds and bonds strongly to other carbon atoms, so chains of many different lengths make families such as the alkanes. Carbon is not the most common element in the crust, and it can form double bonds.

1 mark: so it condenses higher up where the column is cooler
questions.explanation: Heavy fuel oil has larger molecules with higher boiling points, so it condenses lower down where it is hotter.

questions.question: Explain why a fraction is not a pure substance.
markScheme: 1 mark: it contains more than one hydrocarbon / is a mixture
1 mark: of hydrocarbons with similar numbers of carbon atoms and a range of boiling points
questions.explanation: A fraction boils over a range of temperatures because it contains several different hydrocarbons of similar size.

markScheme: 1 mark: they have very high boiling points
1 mark: so they do not evaporate in the heater / condense immediately at the bottom
questions.explanation: Very large molecules have boiling points higher than the temperature reached, so they stay liquid and drain from the bottom.

questions.question: Explain how modern life depends on the products of fractional distillation of crude oil.
markScheme: 1 mark: fuels for transport (petrol, diesel, kerosene for aircraft)
1 mark: fuels for heating / electricity generation (e.g. LPG, heavy fuel oil)
1 mark: feedstock for materials such as polymers, solvents, lubricants and detergents
questions.explanation: Crude oil provides most transport fuels and many everyday materials, including plastics, so modern transport and industry depend on it.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the number of carbon atoms in the molecules of two fractions.
The two fractions overlap in the number of carbon atoms they contain.
Suggest why the fractions are not perfectly separated.

headers: Number of carbon atoms in each molecule

markScheme: 1 mark: hydrocarbons near the boundary have very similar boiling points
1 mark: so some condense in either fraction / temperature ranges overlap
questions.explanation: The boiling points of neighbouring hydrocarbons differ by only a few degrees, so a sharp cut between fractions is not possible.

questions.question: Explain why fractional distillation is described as a physical process rather than a chemical reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: only changes of state (evaporation and condensation) occur
1 mark: no new substances are made / covalent bonds within molecules are not broken
questions.explanation: The same hydrocarbon molecules are present before and after; they are only sorted by boiling point.

questions.question: Describe and explain how crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation.
markScheme: Indicative content: crude oil is heated until it evaporates; the vapour enters the bottom of the fractionating column; the column is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top (temperature gradient); vapours rise and cool; each hydrocarbon condenses when it reaches a level where the temperature is below its boiling point; hydrocarbons with large molecules have high boiling points and condense near the bottom; smaller molecules have lower boiling points and condense higher up; the smallest leave the top as gases; liquid fractions are piped off at different heights; very large molecules form a residue at the bottom; each fraction contains molecules with similar numbers of carbon atoms.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically ordered description that links boiling point to molecule size and to the temperature gradient, using evaporate and condense correctly.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes heating and condensing at different heights with some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. crude oil is heated and fractions come off at different heights.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers link three ideas: the temperature gradient, the boiling point of each hydrocarbon, and molecule size.

questions.question: Crude oil fractions are used both as fuels and as feedstock for the petrochemical industry. Evaluate the use of crude oil to make fuels rather than petrochemicals, given that crude oil is a finite resource.
markScheme: Indicative content: most crude oil is burned as fuel; fuels are essential for transport, heating and electricity; burning fuels uses up the resource permanently; petrochemicals such as polymers, lubricants, solvents and detergents also depend on crude oil; there are alternatives for fuels (e.g. electricity from renewables, biofuels) but fewer for some petrochemicals; conserving crude oil for feedstock may be a better use; a judgement is given.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): considers both uses with reasons and gives a justified conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states uses or simple points without a conclusion.
questions.explanation: An evaluation must weigh up both sides and finish with a reasoned judgement, for example that crude oil is too valuable as a feedstock to burn when alternative fuels exist.

questions.question: Which fraction is collected nearest the top of a fractionating column?
markScheme: 1 mark: liquefied petroleum gases
questions.explanation: LPG contains the smallest molecules (1 to 4 carbon atoms), which have the lowest boiling points and leave the top as gases.

questions.question: State what is meant by 'feedstock'.
markScheme: 1 mark: a raw material used to make other products (in an industrial process)
questions.explanation: Some crude oil fractions are feedstock: raw materials the petrochemical industry turns into polymers, solvents and other products.
